source_batch.unit_label: BFM Module D unit 2 (courseware unit 27): capital adequacy and Basel norms

facts.statement: Three pillars (courseware): the revised Basel framework has three mutually reinforcing pillars: minimum capital requirements (Pillar 1), supervisory review of capital adequacy (Pillar 2) and market discipline (Pillar 3). Pillar 1 offers three options for computing capital for credit risk (standardised approach, foundation internal ratings based approach and advanced internal ratings based approach), options for market risk (standardised approach based on a maturity ladder or duration, and internal models such as VaR) and for operational risk (basic indicator approach, standardised approach and advanced measurement approach); banks choose by risk sensitivity and stage of development. Objective of the revised framework: strengthen soundness and stability, promote stronger risk management and give greater risk sensitivity than the 1988 accord, with incentives for banks with better risk management; regulators may set higher standards. Basel-I was confined to minimum capital for credit (and later market) risk; the revised framework added operational risk, supervisory review and disclosure. Home and host supervisors must cooperate. In India all commercial banks (excluding co-operative banks, local area banks and regional rural banks) were to adopt the standardised approach for credit risk and the basic indicator approach for operational risk, and the standardised duration approach for market risk (as at the courseware date).

Scope of application (courseware): the capital adequacy norms apply to commercial banks on a stand-alone (solo, global) basis and at the consolidated level. A consolidated bank is a group of entities where a licensed bank is the controlling entity; it includes all group entities under its control, except exempted entities, and may exclude group companies engaged in insurance business and businesses not pertaining to financial services. A consolidated bank maintains a minimum capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR) on an ongoing basis.

Pillar 1 minimum capital (courseware, older framework): regulatory capital is Tier I (core: paid-up capital, free reserves and unallocated surplus, less specified deductions) and Tier II (supplementary: subordinated debt of more than five years maturity, loan loss reserves, revaluation reserves, investment fluctuation reserves, limited-life preference shares); the courseware says Tier II is restricted to 100 per cent of Tier I and that Tier III capital, used for market risk in the earlier accord, has been phased out. The total capital ratio must not be lower than 8 per cent (9 per cent in India). Any capital requirement arising from credit and counterparty risk must be met by Tier I and Tier II capital. Total risk-weighted assets = risk-weighted assets for credit risk + 12.5 times the capital requirement for market risk + 12.5 times the capital requirement for operational risk (12.5 is the reciprocal of the minimum 8 per cent). Capital adequacy ratio (CRAR) = regulatory capital / total risk-weighted assets. The framework is more risk sensitive than the 1988 accord. Basel I (1988) set global standards for minimum capital, a revision began in 1999 with a revised framework finalised in 2004 and a comprehensive version in 2006.

Pillar 2 supervisory review (courseware): the capital ratio under Pillar 1 is only the regulatory minimum, covering only credit, market and operational risks; additional capital may be necessary because of some underestimation of risks under Pillar 1 and the actual risk exposure and quality of risk management. Risks not fully captured include interest rate risk in the banking book, credit concentration risk, liquidity risk, settlement risk, reputational risk, strategic risk, risk of under-estimation of credit risk under the standardised approach, model risk under the internal ratings approaches, weakness in credit risk mitigants, residual risk of securitisation, climate risk, and payment and settlement risk, plus factors external to the bank. Banks must make their own assessment of risk exposures through a well-defined internal process and maintain adequate capital: the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP); the supervisor reviews it in the Supervisory Review Process (SRP). Four key principles: (1) banks should have a process for assessing overall capital adequacy in relation to their risk profile and a strategy for maintaining capital levels; (2) supervisors should review and evaluate the bank ICAAP and its compliance with regulatory ratios and take appropriate action if not satisfied; (3) supervisors should expect banks to operate above the minimum and be able to require capital in excess of the minimum; (4) supervisors should intervene at an early stage to prevent capital falling below the minimum and require rapid remedial action. The ICAAP comprises procedures and measures to ensure appropriate identification and measurement of risks, an appropriate level of internal capital in relation to the risk profile and the application and development of suitable risk management systems. Buffers are stipulated for systemic and bank-specific uncertainties.

Structure and features of the ICAAP (courseware): every bank should have an ICAAP, on a solo basis at every tier for each banking entity in the group and at consolidated level; it should encompass firm-wide risk profile with active board and senior management oversight, appropriate policies, procedures and limits, comprehensive identification, measurement, mitigation, control, monitoring and reporting of risks, management information systems and comprehensive internal controls. The ultimate responsibility for design and implementation lies with the board, which sets the tolerance level for risk, ensures senior management has a risk framework and monitoring system, adopts strong internal controls and ensures a strategic plan outlining current and future capital needs, anticipated capital expenditure and desired level of capital. Policies must provide for timely identification, measurement, monitoring, control and mitigation of risks, recognise the economic substance of exposures, be consistent with goals, delineate accountability, escalate breaches, review new products and be reviewed. MIS must be accurate and timely; internal controls independent (risk management function independent of business lines); the ICAAP outcome must be submitted to the board and the central bank and reviewed at least annually. ICAAP must be an integral part of management and decision-making (capital allocation, pricing, expansion and budgets), follow the principle of proportionality, be subject to regular independent review and validation, be forward-looking (capital plan covering needs, anticipated utilisation, desired level, limits and a contingency plan), risk-based (capital targets consistent with risk profile; risks hard to quantify like reputational and strategic risk are treated mainly by qualitative assessment and mitigation), include stress tests and scenario analyses (to evaluate vulnerability to unlikely but plausible events), combine quantitative and qualitative approaches, and assess risk aggregation and diversification effects with caution about correlations. Material risks include credit, market, operational, interest rate risk in the banking book, concentration, liquidity and others. The ICAAP document contains an executive summary, background, current and projected financial and capital positions, capital adequacy (risk appetite, capital needs), firm-wide risk oversight (including off-balance sheet exposures, securitisation, reputational risk, valuation and liquidity risk, stress testing and compensation practices), key sensitivities and scenarios (for example a recession once in 25 years), aggregation and diversification, testing and adoption, and use within the bank.

Pillar 3 market discipline (courseware): the purpose is to complement the minimum capital requirements (Pillar 1) and the supervisory review (Pillar 2) with disclosure requirements that allow market participants to assess key information on the scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment processes and the capital adequacy of the institution, encouraging market discipline and informed decisions. Market discipline contributes to better corporate governance and to a safe banking environment; the courseware quotes the saying that a well-run bank needs no capital and no capital will rescue a badly run bank. Five guiding principles for Pillar 3 disclosures: clear, comprehensive, meaningful to users, consistent over time and comparable across banks. Scope: Pillar 3 applies at the top consolidated level of the banking group; disclosures about individual banks within the group are generally made by the parent, but individual banks that are not the top consolidated entity make Pillar 3 disclosures on a stand-alone basis. Frequency: at least half-yearly, irrespective of whether financial statements are audited, with capital adequacy and credit risk general disclosures and standardised-approach disclosures at least quarterly. Disclosures are included in the published financial results or on the website with a direct link; they should be made concurrently with publication of financial statements. Validation: consistency with audited statements, supplementary material scrutinised internally; external audit is not required unless specified. Materiality: information is material if its omission or misstatement could change or influence the assessment or decision of a user. Proprietary information (which would undermine competitive position) and confidential information (customer data) need not be disclosed in detail but non-disclosure must be stated with reasons. Banks must have a board-approved formal disclosure policy covering what is disclosed, internal controls and validation and frequency. Disclosures are presented in templates (qualitative and quantitative), for example scope of application, capital structure, capital adequacy, credit risk general disclosures, standardised approach portfolios, securitisation, market risk, operational risk, interest rate risk in the banking book and counterparty credit risk; banks also disclose the full terms and conditions of capital instruments on their websites. Circulars of 2010 and 2017 required extra disclosure on HTM sales above a threshold and on divergence in asset classification and provisioning above specified percentages (thresholds not taught).

payload.title: The three pillars of the Basel framework
payload.core_explanation_md:
The revised Basel framework rests on **three mutually reinforcing pillars**:

| Pillar | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Pillar 1: minimum capital requirements** | Risk-sensitive **capital for credit, market and operational risk** with a **choice of approaches** |
| **Pillar 2: supervisory review process** | Banks assess their **own capital adequacy** (**ICAAP**); supervisors **review** it (**SRP**) |
| **Pillar 3: market discipline** | **Disclosures** so the market can judge a bank's **capital and risk** |

**Approaches under Pillar 1:** **credit risk** (standardised, foundation IRB, advanced IRB); **market risk** (standardised: maturity or duration method; internal models such as VaR); **operational risk** (basic indicator, standardised, advanced measurement).

The framework is **more risk sensitive than the 1988 accord** and gives **incentives** to banks with better risk management. **Basel I** covered only minimum capital for credit risk; the revised framework **added operational risk, supervisory review and disclosure**. Home and host supervisors are expected to **cooperate**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Pillar 1 sets the floor, Pillar 2 asks whether the floor is enough, Pillar 3 lets the market check.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline.

payload.title: Scope of application: solo and consolidated
payload.core_explanation_md:
The norms apply to commercial banks **on a stand-alone (solo) basis** and **on a consolidated basis**.

A **consolidated bank** is a **group of entities** under the control of a **licensed bank**. It includes **all group entities it controls**, except exempted ones; it may **exclude insurance** and **non-financial** businesses. It maintains a **minimum CRAR on an ongoing basis**.

The courseware says co-operative banks, local area banks and regional rural banks were outside the scope at its date.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Consolidation stops capital being counted twice inside a group.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a consolidated bank for capital purposes?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A group of entities with a licensed bank as the controlling entity.

payload.title: Pillar 1: regulatory capital and risk-weighted assets (courseware, older framework)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Regulatory capital** (courseware):

- **Tier I (core):** **paid-up capital, free reserves, unallocated surplus**, less deductions.
- **Tier II (supplementary):** **subordinated debt over five years**, **loan loss reserves**, **revaluation reserves**, **investment fluctuation reserves**, **limited-life preference shares**; limited to **100 per cent of Tier I**.
- **Tier III** (once used for market risk) has been **phased out**.

**Minimum total capital ratio** in the courseware: **8 per cent** (**9 per cent in India**). Credit and counterparty risk capital must be met from **Tier I and Tier II**.

**Total risk-weighted assets = RWA for credit risk + 12.5 x capital requirement for market risk + 12.5 x capital requirement for operational risk.** The **12.5** is the **reciprocal of 8 per cent**.

**CRAR = regulatory capital / total risk-weighted assets.**

*The current Basel III components and buffers are taught in the earlier Module B batches; the figures here are the courseware older-framework statements.*
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Multiplying a capital charge by 12.5 converts it into an equivalent risk-weighted asset amount.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the market and operational risk capital multiplied by 12.5?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To convert the capital charge into risk-weighted assets; 12.5 is the reciprocal of the 8 per cent minimum.

payload.title: CRAR and total risk-weighted assets
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Total RWA = RWA(credit) + 12.5 x K(market) + 12.5 x K(operational).**

**CRAR = capital / total RWA x 100.**

**Required capital = minimum ratio x total RWA.**

**Surplus (shortfall) = capital - required capital.**

Example: credit RWA **Rs 8,000 crore**, market capital charge **Rs 40 crore**, operational charge **Rs 60 crore**: total RWA = 8,000 + 500 + 750 = **Rs 9,250 crore**. Capital **Rs 925 crore**: CRAR **10 per cent**.

assumptions: Ratios stated in the question are assumptions
All figures at the same date
common_errors: Adding capital charges directly to RWA without multiplying by 12.5
Using total assets as the denominator

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 12.5 factor puts all three risks on the same footing as risk-weighted assets.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the total RWA if credit RWA is 1,000 and market and operational charges are 10 and 20 (Rs crore)?

payload.title: Pillar 2: ICAAP and the supervisory review process
payload.core_explanation_md:
The Pillar 1 ratio is **only a minimum** and covers **credit, market and operational risk**. Extra capital may be needed because Pillar 1 may **underestimate** risk or because of the bank's **actual risk exposure and risk management quality**.

**Risks not (fully) captured:** **interest rate risk in the banking book**, **credit concentration**, **liquidity**, **settlement**, **reputational**, **strategic**, **model risk**, **weak credit risk mitigants**, **residual securitisation risk**, **climate risk**, and **external factors**.

**ICAAP** (Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process): the **bank's own** process to identify and measure risk, hold **adequate internal capital** for its risk profile and develop **risk management systems**.
**SRP** (Supervisory Review Process): the **supervisor's** review and evaluation of the ICAAP and the bank's compliance.

**Four principles:**

1. Banks need a process to **assess capital against risk profile** and a **strategy to keep it**.
2. Supervisors **review** ICAAP and compliance and **act** if not satisfied.
3. Banks should **operate above the minimum**; supervisors may **require more**.
4. Supervisors should **intervene early** and require **rapid remedial action**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: ICAAP is the bank assessing itself; SRP is the supervisor checking that assessment.

self_check.prompt_text: Which is the bank process and which is the supervisor process: ICAAP or SRP?
self_check.expected_takeaway: ICAAP is the bank internal assessment; SRP is the supervisor review.

payload.title: Features of a sound ICAAP
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Structure:** every bank has an ICAAP, **solo and consolidated**; the **board** carries ultimate responsibility: it sets **risk tolerance**, ensures a **risk framework**, **monitoring**, **strong internal controls** and a **strategic plan** for **current and future capital needs**, **anticipated spending** and **desired capital**.

**Key attributes:**

- **Integral to management:** used in **capital allocation, pricing, expansion and budgets**.
- **Proportionality:** sophistication fits the bank **nature, scale and complexity**.
- **Independent review and validation**; ICAAP outcome **submitted to the board and the central bank** and reviewed **at least annually**.
- **Forward-looking:** a **capital plan** (needs, utilisation, desired level, limits) with a **contingency plan**.
- **Risk-based:** capital targets consistent with the **risk profile**; hard-to-quantify risks (**reputational, strategic**) are handled mainly by **qualitative assessment and mitigation**.
- **Stress tests and scenarios:** test vulnerability to **unlikely but plausible** events (for example a **once-in-25-years recession**).
- **Quantitative and qualitative:** more uncertainty means **more capital cushion**.
- **Aggregation and diversification:** be cautious about **correlations**, which can rise under stress.

**ICAAP document contents:** executive summary, background, current and projected positions, capital adequacy and risk appetite, firm-wide risk oversight, key sensitivities and scenarios, aggregation and diversification, testing and adoption, use within the bank.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Diversification benefits assumed in good times may vanish in stress.

self_check.prompt_text: Who has the ultimate responsibility for the ICAAP?

payload.title: Pillar 3: market discipline and disclosure
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** complement Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 with **disclosure** so market participants can assess **scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment and capital adequacy**; this encourages **market discipline** and **better governance**. (*A well-run bank needs no capital; no capital will rescue a badly run bank.*)

**Five guiding principles:** disclosures should be **clear**, **comprehensive**, **meaningful to users**, **consistent over time** and **comparable across banks**.

| Aspect | Rule (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Scope** | At the **top consolidated level** of the group; individual banks that are not the top entity disclose **on a stand-alone basis** |
| **Frequency** | **At least half-yearly**; capital adequacy and credit risk general and standardised approach disclosures **at least quarterly** |
| **Where** | In **published results** or on the **website** with a **direct link**, **at the same time** as financial results |
| **Validation** | **Consistent with audited statements**; **no external audit required** unless specified |
| **Materiality** | Material if **omission or misstatement could change a user's decision** |
| **Proprietary/confidential** | Need not be disclosed in detail but **non-disclosure must be stated with reasons** |
| **Policy** | A **board-approved disclosure policy** |

Banks also publish the **full terms and conditions of capital instruments** on their websites. Dated circulars on **HTM sales** and **divergence** disclosure are not taught.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Disclosure lets investors and depositors price a bank risk without the regulator doing it for them.

self_check.prompt_text: At what level does Pillar 3 apply to a banking group?

payload.stem_md: A bank has credit RWA of Rs 8,000 crore, a market risk capital charge of Rs 40 crore and an operational risk capital charge of Rs 60 crore. What is the total RWA (Rs crore)?
With regulatory capital of Rs 925 crore, what is the capital adequacy ratio (per cent)?
Assume a minimum capital ratio of 9 per cent for this exercise. What capital is required against total RWA of Rs 9,250 crore (Rs crore, to 2 decimal places)?
With capital of Rs 925 crore and the same requirement, what is the surplus capital (Rs crore, to 2 decimal places)?
Tier I capital is Rs 600 crore and Tier II is Rs 450 crore. If Tier II is limited to 100 per cent of Tier I, how much Tier II counts (Rs crore)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The limit is Rs 600 crore, so all Rs 450 crore of Tier II counts.

payload.stem_md: Tier I capital is Rs 400 crore and Tier II is Rs 700 crore. If Tier II is limited to 100 per cent of Tier I, what is the total regulatory capital (Rs crore)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Tier II counted = min(700, 400) = 400. Total = 400 + 400 = Rs 800 crore.

payload.stem_md: A bank holds capital of Rs 1,100 crore. Its market risk charge is Rs 80 crore and operational risk charge Rs 120 crore, and credit RWA is Rs 10,000 crore. What is its CRAR (per cent, to 2 decimal places)?
A bank has total RWA of Rs 12,500 crore and a market risk charge of Rs 80 crore. What share of total RWA does the market risk part form (per cent)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Market RWA = 12.5 x 80 = 1,000. Share = 1,000 / 12,500 = 8 per cent.

items.title: The three pillars of the Basel framework
items.core_explanation_md:
The revised Basel framework rests on **three mutually reinforcing pillars**:

| Pillar | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Pillar 1: minimum capital requirements** | Risk-sensitive **capital for credit, market and operational risk** with a **choice of approaches** |
| **Pillar 2: supervisory review process** | Banks assess their **own capital adequacy** (**ICAAP**); supervisors **review** it (**SRP**) |
| **Pillar 3: market discipline** | **Disclosures** so the market can judge a bank's **capital and risk** |

**Approaches under Pillar 1:** **credit risk** (standardised, foundation IRB, advanced IRB); **market risk** (standardised: maturity or duration method; internal models such as VaR); **operational risk** (basic indicator, standardised, advanced measurement).

The framework is **more risk sensitive than the 1988 accord** and gives **incentives** to banks with better risk management. **Basel I** covered only minimum capital for credit risk; the revised framework **added operational risk, supervisory review and disclosure**. Home and host supervisors are expected to **cooperate**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Pillar 1 sets the floor, Pillar 2 asks whether the floor is enough, Pillar 3 lets the market check.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Minimum capital requirements, supervisory review and market discipline.

items.title: Scope of application: solo and consolidated
items.core_explanation_md:
The norms apply to commercial banks **on a stand-alone (solo) basis** and **on a consolidated basis**.

A **consolidated bank** is a **group of entities** under the control of a **licensed bank**. It includes **all group entities it controls**, except exempted ones; it may **exclude insurance** and **non-financial** businesses. It maintains a **minimum CRAR on an ongoing basis**.

The courseware says co-operative banks, local area banks and regional rural banks were outside the scope at its date.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Consolidation stops capital being counted twice inside a group.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a consolidated bank for capital purposes?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A group of entities with a licensed bank as the controlling entity.

items.title: Pillar 1: regulatory capital and risk-weighted assets (courseware, older framework)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Regulatory capital** (courseware):

- **Tier I (core):** **paid-up capital, free reserves, unallocated surplus**, less deductions.
- **Tier II (supplementary):** **subordinated debt over five years**, **loan loss reserves**, **revaluation reserves**, **investment fluctuation reserves**, **limited-life preference shares**; limited to **100 per cent of Tier I**.
- **Tier III** (once used for market risk) has been **phased out**.

**Minimum total capital ratio** in the courseware: **8 per cent** (**9 per cent in India**). Credit and counterparty risk capital must be met from **Tier I and Tier II**.

**Total risk-weighted assets = RWA for credit risk + 12.5 x capital requirement for market risk + 12.5 x capital requirement for operational risk.** The **12.5** is the **reciprocal of 8 per cent**.

**CRAR = regulatory capital / total risk-weighted assets.**

*The current Basel III components and buffers are taught in the earlier Module B batches; the figures here are the courseware older-framework statements.*
items.expanded_explanation_md: Multiplying a capital charge by 12.5 converts it into an equivalent risk-weighted asset amount.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the market and operational risk capital multiplied by 12.5?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To convert the capital charge into risk-weighted assets; 12.5 is the reciprocal of the 8 per cent minimum.

items.title: CRAR and total risk-weighted assets
items.core_explanation_md:
**Total RWA = RWA(credit) + 12.5 x K(market) + 12.5 x K(operational).**

**CRAR = capital / total RWA x 100.**

**Required capital = minimum ratio x total RWA.**

**Surplus (shortfall) = capital - required capital.**

Example: credit RWA **Rs 8,000 crore**, market capital charge **Rs 40 crore**, operational charge **Rs 60 crore**: total RWA = 8,000 + 500 + 750 = **Rs 9,250 crore**. Capital **Rs 925 crore**: CRAR **10 per cent**.

All figures at the same date
common_errors: Adding capital charges directly to RWA without multiplying by 12.5
Using total assets as the denominator

items.expanded_explanation_md: The 12.5 factor puts all three risks on the same footing as risk-weighted assets.

items.title: Pillar 2: ICAAP and the supervisory review process
items.core_explanation_md:
The Pillar 1 ratio is **only a minimum** and covers **credit, market and operational risk**. Extra capital may be needed because Pillar 1 may **underestimate** risk or because of the bank's **actual risk exposure and risk management quality**.

**Risks not (fully) captured:** **interest rate risk in the banking book**, **credit concentration**, **liquidity**, **settlement**, **reputational**, **strategic**, **model risk**, **weak credit risk mitigants**, **residual securitisation risk**, **climate risk**, and **external factors**.

**ICAAP** (Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process): the **bank's own** process to identify and measure risk, hold **adequate internal capital** for its risk profile and develop **risk management systems**.
**SRP** (Supervisory Review Process): the **supervisor's** review and evaluation of the ICAAP and the bank's compliance.

**Four principles:**

1. Banks need a process to **assess capital against risk profile** and a **strategy to keep it**.
2. Supervisors **review** ICAAP and compliance and **act** if not satisfied.
3. Banks should **operate above the minimum**; supervisors may **require more**.
4. Supervisors should **intervene early** and require **rapid remedial action**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: ICAAP is the bank assessing itself; SRP is the supervisor checking that assessment.

self_check.prompt_text: Which is the bank process and which is the supervisor process: ICAAP or SRP?
self_check.expected_takeaway: ICAAP is the bank internal assessment; SRP is the supervisor review.

items.title: Features of a sound ICAAP
items.core_explanation_md:
**Structure:** every bank has an ICAAP, **solo and consolidated**; the **board** carries ultimate responsibility: it sets **risk tolerance**, ensures a **risk framework**, **monitoring**, **strong internal controls** and a **strategic plan** for **current and future capital needs**, **anticipated spending** and **desired capital**.

**Key attributes:**

- **Integral to management:** used in **capital allocation, pricing, expansion and budgets**.
- **Proportionality:** sophistication fits the bank **nature, scale and complexity**.
- **Independent review and validation**; ICAAP outcome **submitted to the board and the central bank** and reviewed **at least annually**.
- **Forward-looking:** a **capital plan** (needs, utilisation, desired level, limits) with a **contingency plan**.
- **Risk-based:** capital targets consistent with the **risk profile**; hard-to-quantify risks (**reputational, strategic**) are handled mainly by **qualitative assessment and mitigation**.
- **Stress tests and scenarios:** test vulnerability to **unlikely but plausible** events (for example a **once-in-25-years recession**).
- **Quantitative and qualitative:** more uncertainty means **more capital cushion**.
- **Aggregation and diversification:** be cautious about **correlations**, which can rise under stress.

**ICAAP document contents:** executive summary, background, current and projected positions, capital adequacy and risk appetite, firm-wide risk oversight, key sensitivities and scenarios, aggregation and diversification, testing and adoption, use within the bank.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Diversification benefits assumed in good times may vanish in stress.

items.title: Pillar 3: market discipline and disclosure
items.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** complement Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 with **disclosure** so market participants can assess **scope of application, capital, risk exposures, risk assessment and capital adequacy**; this encourages **market discipline** and **better governance**. (*A well-run bank needs no capital; no capital will rescue a badly run bank.*)

**Five guiding principles:** disclosures should be **clear**, **comprehensive**, **meaningful to users**, **consistent over time** and **comparable across banks**.

| Aspect | Rule (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **Scope** | At the **top consolidated level** of the group; individual banks that are not the top entity disclose **on a stand-alone basis** |
| **Frequency** | **At least half-yearly**; capital adequacy and credit risk general and standardised approach disclosures **at least quarterly** |
| **Where** | In **published results** or on the **website** with a **direct link**, **at the same time** as financial results |
| **Validation** | **Consistent with audited statements**; **no external audit required** unless specified |
| **Materiality** | Material if **omission or misstatement could change a user's decision** |
| **Proprietary/confidential** | Need not be disclosed in detail but **non-disclosure must be stated with reasons** |
| **Policy** | A **board-approved disclosure policy** |

Banks also publish the **full terms and conditions of capital instruments** on their websites. Dated circulars on **HTM sales** and **divergence** disclosure are not taught.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Disclosure lets investors and depositors price a bank risk without the regulator doing it for them.
